<description>
This is a WIP to improve the `MallocUsage` function, with logic to measure actual usage in the unit test code.
</description>

<commits>
8b5b4927f4 memusage: model real malloc implementations in MallocUsage

The previous formula was measured on glibc 2.19 and overestimates the
size of glibc chunks by 16 bytes for half of all request sizes, ignores
glibc's minimum chunk size, and has no notion of mmapped allocations.

Model the allocators actually used by Linux, macOS and Windows builds:
- glibc (ptmalloc2, all Linux release builds): chunks of
  max(MINSIZE, round_up(size + sizeof(size_t), MALLOC_ALIGNMENT)) bytes,
  with chunks of 128 KiB or more mmapped as whole pages. This matches
  glibc 2.43 exactly on x86_64, i386, aarch64, armhf, armel, riscv64,
  ppc64, ppc64le, ppc, s390x, loongarch64, alpha, hppa, m68k, sh4 and
  sparc64 (over 300000 request sizes each).
- musl (mallocng, used by the Alpine CI job): a table of the steady-state
  cost per slot for each of its 48 size classes, including group headers
  and out-of-band metadata, which matches RSS measurements of musl 1.2.5
  within 0.2%.
- macOS (libmalloc): no in-band headers, with requests rounded up to 16
  bytes up to 1008 bytes (tiny/nano), to 512 bytes up to 32 KiB (small),
  to 32 KiB up to 8 MiB (medium), and to whole pages beyond. This matches
  the CI measurements on macOS 15 (arm64) for every size the previous
  estimate got wrong (1-112, 1025-7200 and 32769-493424); the other sizes
  up to 4 MiB were within the test's tolerance. The 8 MiB limit of the
  medium range is libmalloc's default (from its source), not measured.
- Windows x64 (the Windows heap, used by the UCRT's malloc): blocks of
  round_up(size + 8, 16) bytes, except that sizes up to 16 KiB come from
  its low-fragmentation heap, in buckets of 16 to 512 bytes granularity.
  This matches the CI measurements on Windows Server 2022 up to 512 KiB
  (beyond that, addresses no longer reflect usage). Blocks of over
  0xFF000 bytes get their own VirtualAlloc() region, and are counted as
  their committed pages (not measured).

Other platforms (BSDs) keep the previous estimate until they are
measured.

Also count the hash that libc++ stores in every std::unordered_map and
std::unordered_set node, and the second list pointer of MSVC's STL. The
previous MallocUsage() overestimated small allocations enough to hide
this, but with the accurate models, pool_tests/memusage_test fails with
libc++ (it finds that the pool allocator uses more memory than
std::allocator, as the std_map nodes are counted as 24 instead of 32
bytes), and would with MSVC.

That test also assumes that malloc has a per-allocation overhead, which
the pool allocator avoids. macOS's allocator has none for small blocks,
so there the pool really uses slightly more memory (for the list of its
chunks). Only check that the pool saves memory where malloc's overhead
for the nodes is significant.

04f59b28a0 test: compare MallocUsage against measured allocator behaviour

Add a unit test that measures how much memory malloc() actually consumes
and fails if MallocUsage() is more than a factor 1+1/16 below, or more
than a factor 1+1/8 above, the measured usage. The upper bound is looser
because MallocUsage() may include out-of-band allocator metadata that
the measurement does not see (up to 1/8 for musl's smallest size class).

By default, a random set of sizes up to 4 MiB (512 KiB on Windows, see
below) is tested: for every power of two 2^b, 16 >> (b / 4) (but at
least one) sizes in [2^b, 2^(b+1)), so small sizes are tested more
densely than large ones. Every mismatching size is reported on its own
line, with its measured usage.

When the ALL_SIZES constant is set to true, the test instead determines
the usage of every size up to 4 MiB (searching for the boundaries
between size classes, assuming usage does not decrease with size),
reports mismatching size ranges, and prints the results in a form meant
for writing MallocUsage() code, e.g. for glibc on x86_64:

  1-24: 32
  25-131048: round_up(size + 8, 16)
  131049-4194280: round_up(size + 24, 4096)

This takes about 25 seconds with glibc, and 5 with musl. In this mode,
glibc's mmap threshold is pinned to its default, as glibc otherwise
raises it whenever an mmapped block is freed, which would make the
results depend on the order of the measurements.

The usage of a size is measured as the smallest distance between
neighbouring blocks (in address order), among up to 16384 live
allocations of that size, that accounts for at least 10% of all pairs.
This is robust against a fragmented heap (the test binary's heap holds
over a thousand regularly spaced free holes at startup, which dominate
smaller samples) and against allocators that place blocks at varying
offsets within their slots (musl).

Large blocks are often given page-granular memory, with the block at an
offset within it that varies from block to block (musl cycles it), which
makes neighbouring blocks slightly closer than the memory they use. Such
an allocator returns a different address, less than a page away, when a
block is freed and allocated again. If that happens (for distances of a
page or more), the test also looks at the longest run of neighbours
whose distances are within a page of that distance. If all of them lie
within less than a page of a grid whose spacing is a multiple of the
page size, that spacing is the usage. Blocks that are really spaced by
something else (e.g. glibc's 4080-byte chunks) drift away from any such
grid, though not necessarily within a short run (such as within one
Windows heap segment), which is why this is only done when the offsets
are seen to vary. Without this, musl's output in the ALL_SIZES mode has
two lines per page above its mmap threshold, one of them 16 bytes too
low; with it, the output is:

  1-12: 16
  13-156: round_up(size + 4, 16)
  157-188: 192
  ... (one line per size class) ...
  104829-131036: 131072
  131037-131051: 131056
  131052-131052: 131072
  131053-4194284: round_up(size + 20, 4096)

On Windows, only sizes up to 512 KiB are tested: larger blocks often get
their own heap segment or VirtualAlloc() region, so the distances
between them reflect reserved address space rather than usage.

Sanitizer builds are skipped, as MallocUsage() does not model their
allocators.

60524a8d93 test: measure every allocation size in memusage_tests

Enable ALL_SIZES, so that the malloc_usage test measures the usage of
every allocation size up to 4 MiB (instead of a random sample) and prints
the results in a form meant for writing MallocUsage() code. This takes
about 25 seconds with glibc, and 5 with musl.
</commits>
